1 import { TipGood, TipBad, TipInfo } from "@/components/tips"; 2 import { Iframe } from "@/components/iframe"; 3 import { Example } from "@/components/example"; 4 import { Figure } from "@/components/figure"; 5 import { CodeExampleStack } from "@/components/code-example"; 6 7 export const title = "Detecting classes in source files"; 8 export const description = "Understanding and customizing how Tailwind scans your source files."; 9 10 ## Overview 11 12 Tailwind works by scanning your project for utility classes, then generating all of the necessary CSS based on the classes you've actually used. 13 14 This makes sure your CSS is as small as possible, and is also what makes features like [arbitrary values](/docs/adding-custom-styles#using-arbitrary-values) possible. 15 16 ### How classes are detected 17 18 Tailwind treats all of your source files as plain text, and doesn't attempt to actually parse your files as code in any way. 19 20 Instead it just looks for any tokens in your file that could be classes based on which characters Tailwind is expecting in class names: 21 22 ```jsx 23 // [!code filename:JSX] 24 // [!code word:bg-blue-500] 25 // [!code word:rounded-full] 26 // [!code word:text-white] 27 // [!code word:text-black] 28 // [!code word:font-medium] 29 // [!code word:text-sm\/6] 30 // [!code word:font-sans] 31 // [!code word:bg-black] 32 // [!code word:bg-white] 33 // [!code word:className] 34 // [!code word:function] 35 // [!code word:children] 36 // [!code word:button] 37 // [!code word:shadow] 38 // [!code word:export] 39 // [!code word:colors] 40 // [!code word:color] 41 // [!code word:black] 42 // [!code word:white] 43 // [!code word:const] 44 // [!code word:blue] 45 // [!code word:return] 46 // [!code word:py-1.5] 47 // [!code word:px-2] 48 export function Button({ color, children }) { 49 const colors = { 50 black: "bg-black text-white", 51 blue: "bg-blue-500 text-white", 52 white: "bg-white text-black", 53 }; 54 55 return ( 56 59 ); 60 } 61 ``` 62 63 Then it tries to generate the CSS for all of these tokens, throwing away any tokens that don't map to a utility class the framework knows about. 64 65 ### Dynamic class names 66 67 Since Tailwind scans your source files as plain text, it has no way of understanding string concatenation or interpolation in the programming language you're using. 68 69 {<>Don't construct class names dynamically} 70 71 ```html 72 73
74 ``` 75 76 In the example above, the strings `text-red-600` and `text-green-600` do not exist, so Tailwind will not generate those classes. 77 78 Instead, make sure any class names you’re using exist in full: 79 80 {<>Always use complete class names} 81 82 ```html 83 84 85 86
87 ``` 88 89 If you're using a component library like React or Vue, this means you shouldn't use props to dynamically construct classes: 90 91 Don't use props to build class names dynamically 92 93 ```jsx 94 // [!code filename:JSX] 95 function Button({ color, children }) { 96 return ; 97 } 98 ``` 99 100 Instead, map props to complete class names that are statically detectable at build-time: 101 102 Always map props to static class names 103 104 ```jsx 105 // [!code filename:JSX] 106 function Button({ color, children }) { 107 const colorVariants = { 108 blue: "bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-500", 109 red: "bg-red-600 hover:bg-red-500", 110 }; 111 112 return ; 113 } 114 ``` 115 116 This has the added benefit of letting you map different prop values to different color shades for example: 117 118 ```jsx 119 // [!code filename:JSX] 120 function Button({ color, children }) { 121 const colorVariants = { 122 blue: "bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-500 text-white", 123 red: "bg-red-500 hover:bg-red-400 text-white", 124 yellow: "bg-yellow-300 hover:bg-yellow-400 text-black", 125 }; 126 127 return ; 128 } 129 ``` 130 131 As long as you always use complete class names in your code, Tailwind will generate all of your CSS perfectly every time. 132 133 ### Which files are scanned 134 135 Tailwind will scan every file in your project for class names, except in the following cases: 136 137 - Files that are in your `.gitignore` file 138 - Files in the `node_modules` directory 139 - Binary files like images, videos, or zip files 140 - CSS files 141 - Common package manager lock files 142 143 If you need to scan any files that Tailwind is ignoring by default, you can [explicitly register](#explicitly-registering-sources) those sources. 144 145 ## Explicitly registering sources 146 147 Use `@source` to explicitly register source paths relative to the stylesheet: 148 149 ```css 150 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 151 @import "tailwindcss"; 152 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 153 @source "../node_modules/@acmecorp/ui-lib"; 154 ``` 155 156 This is especially useful when you need to scan an external library that is built with Tailwind, since dependencies are usually listed in your `.gitignore` file and ignored by Tailwind by default. 157 158 ### Setting your base path 159 160 Tailwind uses the current working directory as its starting point when scanning for class names by default. 161 162 To set the base path for source detection explicitly, use the `source()` function when importing Tailwind in your CSS: 163 164 ```css 165 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 166 /* [!code word:source("../src")] */ 167 @import "tailwindcss" source("../src"); 168 ``` 169 170 This can be useful when working with monorepos where your build commands run from the root of the monorepo instead of the root of each project. 171 172 ### Ignoring specific paths 173 174 Use `@source not` to ignore specific paths, relative to the stylesheet, when scanning for class names: 175 176 ```css 177 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 178 @import "tailwindcss"; 179 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 180 @source not "../src/components/legacy"; 181 ``` 182 183 This is useful when you have large directories in your project that you know don't use Tailwind classes, like legacy components or third-party libraries. 184 185 ### Disabling automatic detection 186 187 Use `source(none)` to completely disable automatic source detection if you want to register all of your sources explicitly: 188 189 ```css 190 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 191 /* [!code word:source("../src")] */ 192 @import "tailwindcss" source(none); 193 194 @source "../admin"; 195 @source "../shared"; 196 ``` 197 198 This can be useful in projects that have multiple Tailwind stylesheets where you want to make sure each one only includes the classes each stylesheet needs. 199 200 ## Safelisting specific utilities

content.text:
This confirms the root cause: Tailwind scans source files as plain text and can't resolve `{{ Vite::image('hero.jpg') }}` inside an arbitrary value at build time, so `bg-[url('...')]` never gets generated — that's a "dynamic class name," which Tailwind explicitly doesn't support.

**Docs:** `src/docs/detecting-classes-in-source-files.mdx`, "Dynamic class names" section (lines 65–131).

Your inline `style="background-image: url(...)"` fix is the correct workaround since the value is only known at render time (server-side, from Vite). The docs recommend mapping to complete static class names when possible, but for runtime-computed URLs like this, inline `style` is the standard approach — Tailwind's plain-text scanner simply can't see inside Blade interpolation.
